In brief

As Bloom gazes at poplin fabric in a Grafton Street shop window he thinks, "Must be washed in rainwater." Perhaps he is looking at a display card with washing instructions for the cloth, or it could be that he is remembering such instructions. The placement of this sentence in his interior monologue suggests that he is also thinking of a phrase from the beginning of Lestrygonians, "washed in the blood of the lamb."

At more length

Gifford plausibly supposes that "Bloom sees in the window part of a sign with instructions for the care of the cloth. Rainwater was widely used with delicate materials and unstable dyes because it was ideally soft (i.e., contained no minerals)." Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that the practice was recommended more generally—"Rainwater was often recommended for washing clothes: 'Save all the rainwater you can get for washing clothes. Scarcely any soap is then required' (Leinster Express, 18 May 1918)"—but the "Must" in Bloom's sentence, and the rich red color of the fabric he is staring at, probably argue for Gifford's view that the instruction is specific to this one fabric.

All of that is very concrete and practical, but the placement of the sentence in the middle of Bloom's recollection of an operatic scene celebrating mass murder invites other associations. The poplin is "bloodhued," the color of "lustrous blood," and it pours from the mouth of an urn in a "flood." Even without the insistence on how the cloth must be washed, this flood of blood might be enough to make readers recall a flood of blood earlier in the chapter: "Are you saved? All are washed in the blood of the lamb. God wants blood victim." It would seem, then, that garment care instructions interrupt Bloom's operatic reverie because ever since the beginning of the chapter he has been thinking, consciously or unconsciously, about God's wish to see people washed, not in rainwater, but in blood.

John Hunt 2026
